questions.q: Per this lesson, why do experienced reviewers often ask deliberately underspecified questions?
options: Because they forgot to include all the necessary details
Because real production environments are full of missing information, and the board wants to see how a candidate operates when a requirement isn't fully specified
Because fully specified questions are against review board rules
Because ambiguous questions are always easier for the board to score
questions.explain: Ambiguity in a question is often deliberate -- it mirrors real production conditions where requirements are rarely fully specified, and tests whether a candidate freezes or works productively with incomplete information.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say silently picking one interpretation of an ambiguous question and answering it is the weakest response?
options: Because the board always already knows which interpretation you picked
Because answering silently is explicitly against the rules of every review board
Because if the silent guess is wrong, the entire answer gets evaluated against a question that wasn't actually asked, and the board never got the chance to correct it
Because silent assumptions are always factually incorrect
questions.explain: A silent guess risks the whole subsequent answer being evaluated against the wrong question, with no chance for the board to correct a wrong assumption before the answer is built on it.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'load-bearing' assumption from an incidental one, per this lesson?
options: A load-bearing assumption is any assumption made at all, regardless of impact
Load-bearing assumptions only apply to security-related questions
A load-bearing assumption would change the answer significantly if it turned out to be wrong; an incidental one wouldn't, and doesn't need to be stated out loud every time
There is no meaningful distinction -- all assumptions should be stated with equal emphasis
questions.explain: The judgment call is identifying which assumptions actually change the substance of the answer if wrong (load-bearing, worth stating explicitly) versus minor details that don't materially change anything (incidental, not worth litigating out loud every time).

questions.q: Why does this lesson say reasoning out loud can matter more than the final answer itself for a genuinely ambiguous question?
options: Because the board is only interested in how long an answer takes to give
Because a board evaluating an ambiguous question is often more interested in the visible thinking process and judgment than in which single defensible answer is reached
Because final answers are never evaluated in a review board setting
Because reasoning out loud always produces the one objectively correct answer
questions.explain: When a question genuinely has more than one defensible answer, narrating the reasoning lets the board evaluate judgment and thought process, not just a final sentence -- a reasoned path to a defensible conclusion is easier to evaluate than an unexplained correct-sounding answer.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is asking a clarifying question the better move than stating an assumption and proceeding?
options: Always -- clarifying questions should be asked for every ambiguity, no matter how small
Never -- clarifying questions should be avoided entirely in a review board
When the two interpretations would lead to genuinely different designs, not just different details within the same design, since guessing wrong would waste real time building the wrong branch
Only when the reviewer explicitly invites a clarifying question first
questions.explain: Stating an assumption works when either interpretation leads to a similar design; asking is better when the interpretations diverge into genuinely different designs, where a wrong guess wastes real time. Asking about every small ambiguity, on the other hand, turns the session into interviewing the board instead of being evaluated.
